newsitem.title: UK: Moody's publishes report on German life insurers.
newsitem.headline: Moody's publishes report on German life insurers.

text.p: LONDON, April 30 - In its recent report entitled German Life Insurance Industry Outlook, Moody's Investors Service recognises the significant fundamental financial and business strengths of German life insurers, and the benefits that the industry derived in the past from the economic, regulatory, accounting, and tax environment.

"But, over the medium-term, heightened competition, decreased regulatory supervision, and an uncertain outlook for sales growth will have destabilising effects on the industry and will have a negative impact on the sector's credit risk outlook."

Clear Advantages for Domestic Players In the near term, German life insurers' current dominance of domestic distribution channels, their operating efficiency, and their financial strength are competitive advantages over all new entrants.
German insurers for the most part, until now, had loyal client bases, low investment risk profiles, and conservative capital structures.

Moody's also notes, that the life insurance industry will benefit going forward from an increasing need for private retirement savings as the government is being forced to reduce the generous benefits available under the current state pension and social security schemes.
Moody's cautions, however, that the new trend towards defined contribution pensions will not benefit life insurers alone.

As the government has proposed to cut substantially the current tax benefits available to life insurance, Moody's is concerned that the attractiveness of the product may be substantially reduced, and that competition from other forms of savings will increase dramatically, especially from mutual funds targeted at pension savings.

Financial Strength is Affected by Shifts in Distribution and Products Moody's says, that premium rate and product liberalization, which results from the deregulation of German life insurance in 1994, destabilizes operating cash flows, produces shifts in customer loyalty, reduces the companies' ability to reserve as conservatively as in the past, and makes earnings more volatile.

The rating agency adds, that as new local and foreign competitors challenge existing franchises, other forms of distribution such as brokers, direct sales, and cooperation between banks and insurers will become more important.
As a result, many life insurers face the challenge of establishing more efficient distribution through diverse channels without upsetting their existing sales force.

Moody's continues to say, that in the near term, the industry may rely on its profitable non-linked product structure, but the competitive environment will erode the market share of these products (endowments) over the long term.

Moody's expects the trend towards protection products (term and disability) and annuities to continue, as well as the importance of unit-linked insurance to increase. "Some of these developments are likely to erode profit margins.
To effectively protect their margins in the long run, German life insurers therefore need to be cost-effective," says the rating agency.

Moody's is concerned, however, that insurers could also turn to more aggressive strategies in investment management and elsewhere, as the potential to cut costs is limited given the need to maintain expensive distribution systems, and the difficulty to cut the cost of labor given the current labor and social security laws.

Consolidation Within the Industry Will Pick Up Moody's report states that in the long run, consolidation will eliminate the weaker insurers, especially those which lack the critical mass to operate or to expand independently, and which may find that the former tight system of regulation was the main factor keeping them in business.

Increased competition will create a much greater dispersion in the financial strength of life insurers than we see today. A Diverse Industry The report, which includes statistics for forty large German life insurers, emphasises the wide range of business mixes and positions, investment portfolios, profitability, and capital strength characteristics of these insurers.

Against this background, it is not surprising that some companies will adapt less easily than others to changing conditions, and that a widening range of creditworthiness will characterise the sector. In future, policyholders, investors, bank counterparties, and insurance brokers may need to analyse more in-depth the relative strengths of German life insurers.
